extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers; students of philosophy/literature; readers of Montaigne
extracted.subtask_description: An essay (Montaigne's 'Of Experience') offering practical moral and medical maxims about self-knowledge, custom, health, speech, and advising others — reflective guidance rather than formal rules. Extracts prescriptive principles the author advances for living, judging, and advising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of knowledge / modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Neither they who know are to enquire, forasmuch as they know; nor they who do not know, forasmuch as to enquire they must know what they enquire of.’ — learning should make one sensible how much one has to learn; modesty and coldness of opinion are virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that true learning reveals ignorance; one should cultivate modesty, avoid arrogant, self-assured assertions, and resist ‘troublesome and wrangling arrogance’ that blocks discipline and truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assert before knowing (avoid premature affirmation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted maxim: “Nihil est turpius, quam cognitioni et perceptions assertionem approbationemque praecurrere.” (‘Nothing is worse than that assertion and decision should precede knowledge and perception.’)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirmation and obstinacy are signs of lack of wit; avoid stubborn assertions even after repeated adverse experience (the coxcomb who persists despite knocks). Favor inquiry over premature decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge others only with knowledge, benevolence, and boldness
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Plato requires three things in him who will examine the soul of another: knowledge, benevolence, boldness.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To criticize or correct another (especially intimately) one must understand the subject, intend well, and have the courage to speak plainly; otherwise such judgments are unfair or harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speak truth circumspectly (timing and limits to truth-telling)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Truth itself has not the privilege to be spoken at all times and indiscriminately; its use... has its circumspections and limits.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even virtuous remonstrance can be injuriously or unjustly applied; consider consequences and context before telling hard truths — especially to those in power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for a royal/confidential adviser
rubrics_metrics.description: An adviser to a prince should be content with his own fortune, of moderate station, limited to one person, and hold fidelity of silence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne advises independence (not seeking preferment), social accessibility (moderate station for easier communication), confidentiality (fidelity of silence), and that the office be vested in one trusted person to avoid irreverence and self-interest among multiple advisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer firsthand observation over blind appeal to books/authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne values what he has seen as much as what is written: he quotes authorities but often prefers to ‘quote a friend’ or what he has seen, holding that age alone does not make truth wiser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t dignify a claim merely because it is printed; empirical observation and common examples from life can be as or more instructive than learned citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom shapes character and tolerances — respect habitual practices
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Tis for custom to give a form to a man’s life… she can mould us…’ and the author keeps the same bed, hours, meat, and drink in sickness and in health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When prescribing change (especially medical), account for ingrained habits: sudden alterations often do harm. In sickness keep as much of accustomed routine as possible and avoid imposing contrary methods on those long accustomed to another life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain habitual routine in sickness where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘My form of life is the same in sickness as in health; the same bed, the same hours, the same meat, and even the same drink, serve me in both conditions alike…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne finds continuity less disruptive than alternating between the extremes of fortune and medical prescriptions; moderate adjustments only as needed for strength or appetite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward medical dogma; expect diversity of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The art of physic is not so fixed… The diversity of medical arguments and opinions embraces all sorts and forms.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physicians vary by climate, method, and time; if one physician forbids something, find another who will not. Do not assume a single medical doctrine is absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let nature take its course; avoid over-intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘We ought to grant free passage to diseases; I find they stay less with me, who let them alone… Let us a little permit Nature to take her own way; she better understands her own affairs than we.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne reports recovering from maladies by nonintervention; aggressive attempts to cut short a disease can lengthen or worsen it. Exercise appropriate patience and restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid remedies worse than the disease; favor pleasure where harmless
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘I hate remedies that are more troublesome than the disease itself… If it be a delicious medicine, take it: ’tis always so much present good.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh burdens of treatment against benefits; do not impose painful or joyless regimens if they outweigh the disease's harm; the pleasantness of a remedy counts as a kind of profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate flexibility and avoid over-fastidiousness / rigid rules
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The worst quality in a well-bred man is over-fastidiousness… It is in every man unbecoming, but in a soldier vicious and intolerable.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be adaptable to customs and circumstances; young men should vary their rules to preserve vigor. Excessive adherence to particular ways makes one inept in diverse situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt tone and mode of speech to audience and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Speak according to the affair you are speaking about to your auditor… There is a certain voice accommodated to the hearing, not by its loudness, but by its propriety.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control voice, tone, and motion to instruct, flatter, or reprehend; speaking is half the speaker and half the hearer — consider the listener’s readiness and role in receiving speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience is the truest test in arts (including medicine)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Physic itself professes always to have experience for the test of its operations… to be a right physician… should first himself have passed through all the diseases he pretends to cure.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical experience (living through conditions) provides essential judgment for practitioners; theoretical knowledge alone may be insufficient to guide real action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be patient with life’s evils; do not be ruined by impatience
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Experience has, moreover, taught me this, that we ruin ourselves by impatience… Evils have their life and limits, their diseases and their recovery.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that afflictions have natural courses and limits; impatience and frantic efforts may prolong or worsen problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect cultural and individual differences in regimen and tolerances
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: chestnuts may not hurt a Perigordin; different nations tolerate different bedding and heat; what is wholesome for one may harm another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medical and behavioral prescriptions should be individualized: climate, upbringing, and custom determine what is tolerable or harmful; universal prescriptions are suspect.
